opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons. The biggest one is probably the pretraining data. The Qwen team seems to have put a lot of math, code, and reasoning-heavy content into pretraining, and likely a fair amount of synthetic data from stronger models too. So by the time you get the base or instruct model, a lot of the reasoning capability is already latent in there. It just hasn't been fully elicited yet.

That's really how we think about it with something like s1. We only fine-tuned on about a thousand carefully selected reasoning traces, which is tiny. Seeing large gains from that little data strongly suggests we're not teaching the model to reason from scratch. We're unlocking or formatting a behavior that's already there. If you try the same recipe on a model whose pretraining didn't include that kind of data, you don't get nearly the same jump.

There are also practical reasons. Qwen comes in a nice range of sizes, so you can study scaling. The 32B model is a sweet spot: strong enough to do interesting things on hard benchmarks like AIME or GPQA, but still feasible to fine-tune on an academic budget in well under an hour on a handful of GPUs. And the weights are openly available, which matters a lot for reproducibility. We wanted everything we released, including data, code, and model, to be something anyone could rerun.

I'd add one caveat. Because so much of the capability comes from pretraining, you have to be careful how you interpret results. When people say "we got reasoning with only a thousand examples," the honest framing is that you got it on top of a base model that had already seen an enormous amount of relevant data. That's still a really useful finding. It means post-training for reasoning can be very cheap. But a lot of the credit belongs to the base model.

r001.rationale: It says Qwen pretraining included substantial math, code, and reasoning-heavy content, which supports suitability for reasoning experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually a really interesting question, and it ties into one of the main findings we had in s1. When we started the project, we tried a bunch of different base models, and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct ended up being the one where everything just clicked. We fine-tuned it on only a thousand examples, and it got close to o1-preview on things like AIME and MATH. But when we tried the exact same thousand examples on other models, it often didn't work nearly as well.

So I think the honest answer is that the base model already has most of the reasoning capability inside it. Qwen was trained on a huge amount of math and code data, and there's a lot of evidence that it has seen long chain-of-thought style traces during pretraining or in its post-training. What our fine-tuning does is really more like activating a format. We're teaching it to think for longer, to put its reasoning in a thinking section, to double check itself, and the model already knows how to do the underlying steps. That's why a thousand examples is enough. You're not teaching it new math, you're teaching it how to use what it already has.

This also connects to budget forcing, our test-time scaling method. When we append "Wait" to make the model keep thinking, Qwen actually uses that extra compute productively. It goes back and catches mistakes. Some weaker base models, when you force them to continue, just ramble or repeat themselves, so the extra tokens don't convert into accuracy. Qwen has enough latent capability that the scaling curve actually goes up as you give it more thinking time.

And then there's the practical side. It's open weights, the 32B size is big enough to be strong but small enough that academic labs can train it with a handful of GPUs in about half an hour, and the Qwen team releases things permissively. So for an experiment where the whole point is to show that simple, cheap methods can get you a lot of the way there, Qwen was kind of the ideal starting point. I'd just add the caveat that this means some of what people attribute to our data or our method is really the base model, and I think the field should be careful about disentangling those two things.

astra-6.text: I think Qwen is a strong starting point because it already has a lot of the capabilities you need for reasoning, particularly in math and coding. So you’re not trying to teach it everything from scratch—you’re building on knowledge and skills that are already there. And having open weights makes it much easier to experiment, compare approaches, and let other researchers reproduce what you’re doing. That doesn’t mean it’s the only model that would work, but it’s a very useful base for studying how to elicit and improve reasoning.

sol-6.1.text: I think the main thing is that you want a base model that already has strong capabilities, especially in math and code. Then you can explore whether reasoning training helps the model use those capabilities more effectively. Qwen is a strong starting point for that, and having the weights openly available makes it much easier to run controlled experiments and let other people reproduce the results.
